title: SQL Server and on-premises modernization
summary: One nightly SQL Server job, taken apart: inventory it, decompose its procedure and package, reproduce the semantics that decide its numbers, reconcile old and new, and cut over on evidence.
outcomes: Inventory a stored procedure, an SSIS-style package and its Agent schedule, including the clock, collation, watermark, temporary objects and transaction scope.
Decompose the procedure into tested target steps and map precedence constraints and schedules onto job tasks, dependencies and run-if conditions.
Choose target keys, outer-join filters, business-day clocks, integer arithmetic and money types that reproduce the legacy meaning, and name the check that proves each.
Reconcile old and new paths on one basis and plan coexistence, cutover and rollback against stated criteria.
startingAssumptions: You read SQL joins, grouping and three-valued NULL logic comfortably.
The architecture and ingestion modules have introduced staged migration, idempotent pipelines and reconciliation of business state.
editorialRationale: SQL Server migrations fail when syntax conversion is mistaken for semantic migration, so the module starts from one small original pipeline, inventories the settings that decide its results, decomposes the procedure and package into tested steps, and then treats identity, triggers, transactions, temporary objects, incremental state, data types, NULL rules, collation and the business-day clock as separate decisions. A deliberately non-equivalent translation, executed in Lab L24 on local Spark, shows which reconciliation check catches each wrong choice before coexistence and cutover turn the evidence into a decision.

concepts.definition: A record of every object, dependency, setting, owner and schedule a workload relies on, written before any translation.
concepts.example: Cinderline's inventory lists sp_daily_inspections, its four source tables, the server clock, the CI_AS collation and etl.watermark.

concepts.definition: Splitting one stored procedure into target steps that each have one input, one output and one executable check.
concepts.example: Select window, rebuild detail, aggregate report and advance watermark become four steps with four tests.

concepts.definition: Translating package tasks, precedence constraints and schedules into job tasks, dependencies, run-if conditions and triggers.
concepts.example: Three Failure constraints joined by OR become one task that runs when at least one dependency failed.

concepts.definition: Two paths are equivalent when they produce the same rows and values on the same basis, not when their code has the same shape.
concepts.example: The line-by-line translation compiles and returns six report rows, yet fails the key, totals, null and type checks.

concepts.definition: A column whose values the database generates on insert; unique, but not guaranteed consecutive on either platform.
concepts.example: inspection_id values 101 to 112 may have gaps after a restart without anything being lost.

concepts.definition: Code the database runs automatically on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, whose effects are part of the table's behaviour.
concepts.example: trg_inspection_touch sets updated_at on every update, which is what the watermark depends on.

concepts.definition: The rule for what a transaction may see of other transactions' uncommitted or concurrent changes.
concepts.example: READ COMMITTED with locking on the source; WriteSerializable by default on a Delta target.

concepts.definition: The set of writes that commit together or not at all; everything outside it can be seen half-done.
concepts.example: The legacy job rebuilds detail, merges the report and moves the watermark inside one transaction.

concepts.definition: A session-scoped table or view that exists only while its session or procedure runs.
concepts.example: #affected_days lives only inside the procedure's session; ##line_handoff is read by another session.

concepts.definition: A stored position, such as the last loaded moment, that decides which changed rows the next incremental run selects.
concepts.example: etl.watermark holds 2026-03-03 06:30; tonight selects rows updated after it and up to 06:30 on 4 March.

concepts.definition: Source features that record which rows changed (change tracking) or the changed data itself (change data capture), including deletes.
concepts.example: A deleted inspection leaves no updated_at to find, but change tracking records its key.

concepts.definition: DATETIME is a SQL Server local date-time rounded to 1/300 second with no offset; TIMESTAMP is an instant shown in a session zone; TIMESTAMP_NTZ has no zone.
concepts.example: 05:59:59.999 stored as DATETIME reads 06:00:00.000; as TIMESTAMP_NTZ it stays 05:59:59.999.

concepts.definition: Money kept in a fixed-precision decimal type so sums are exact at the declared scale.
concepts.example: 0.10 + 0.20 is 0.30 as DECIMAL and 0.30000000000000004 as DOUBLE.

concepts.definition: The rules a database uses to decide whether two strings are equal and how they sort.
concepts.example: Under CI_AS, 'qa07' and 'QA07 ' equal 'QA07', but ' QA07' with a leading space does not.

concepts.definition: The rules for comparisons, joins, functions and filters when a value is NULL, which differ in corners between engines.
concepts.example: CONCAT('P1','-',NULL) is 'P1-' in T-SQL and NULL with Spark's concat.

concepts.definition: A reporting day that starts at a cutoff such as 06:00 on a named clock; the clock must be explicit on the target.
concepts.example: Inspection 103 at 02:10 local belongs to 2 March; computed from a UTC session it lands on 3 March.

concepts.definition: A comparison of two paths on one basis: counts, keys, totals, nulls and types, with every difference explained or failed.
concepts.example: Binary keys pass row counts and day totals but fail the keyed comparison on 3 March.

concepts.definition: A period in which the legacy and new paths both run on the same basis and the old path keeps serving users.
concepts.example: The Agent job keeps feeding the morning report while the new job runs after it and reconciles.

concepts.definition: The switch of consumers to the new path after stated criteria are met, with a rehearsed way back.
concepts.example: Five clean days after the last code change, owned exceptions and a rehearsed rollback open the gate.

concepts.definition: A named SQL routine stored in Unity Catalog and run with CALL, on Databricks Runtime 17.0 or later.
concepts.example: CALL quality.rebuild_days('P1') could wrap the four target steps in one routine.

concepts.definition: Several SQL statements over several Unity Catalog managed tables that commit or roll back together.
concepts.example: Detail, report and watermark updates inside one BEGIN ATOMIC block.

concepts.definition: A Databricks collation that compares strings case-insensitively after lower-casing, keeping accents distinct.
concepts.example: inspector_code STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE makes 'qa07' equal 'QA07'.

concepts.definition: A Databricks Labs toolkit with analyze, transpile and reconcile commands for migrations to Databricks.
concepts.example: Its reconcile step compares a SQL Server table with its Databricks copy.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's first inventory lists 14 procedures, 3 packages and 22 reports with owners and schedules. Which addition most likely prevents a 'reconciliation failure' surfacing mid-pilot?

options.text: The row count of every table, since equal counts on both sides prove the translation.
options.rationale: Lab L24's line-by-line translation returns six report rows like the legacy job and still fails keys, totals, nulls and types.

options.text: The server clock, the column collations and the watermark each procedure relies on.
options.rationale: These settings decide which day a row lands on, which codes join and which rows a run reads; leaving them out lets two correct-looking paths disagree.

options.text: The runtime of each procedure, since a slower target job would produce different numbers.
options.rationale: Runtime matters for the schedule, but a slow job counts the same rows; it is a capacity question, not a meaning question.

options.text: The layout of each report page, since consumers compare the pages side by side.
options.rationale: Layout is presentation; two identically formatted reports can disagree on every number beneath them.

questions.prompt: A translation joins inspector codes with plain equality instead of the source collation's rule. Row counts and per-day totals match the legacy report. Which check fails, and why?

options.text: The null-count check, because unmatched codes become NULL in the output.
options.rationale: The shift is replaced by UNASSIGNED, so no NULL appears in the report; in Lab L24 this flip passes the null check.

options.text: The type check, because a binary string comparison changes the column type.
options.rationale: The comparison rule changes which rows match, not the declared type of any output column.

options.text: No check fails: equal totals prove equivalence at the grain that is reported.
options.rationale: The reported grain is plant, day and shift; totals per day are a coarser grain that hides movement between shifts.

options.text: The keyed comparison: rows moved from DAY to UNASSIGNED within the same day, so group values changed while day totals stayed equal.
options.rationale: Inspections 104 and 105 change shift but not day; only a comparison keyed by plant, day and shift sees 300 become 110 units for DAY.

questions.prompt: Three package tasks each have a Failure precedence constraint into Notify on failure, combined with logical OR. How should the job plan express that task?

options.text: Depend on all three tasks and run when at least one dependency failed.
options.rationale: This keeps the package's promise: mail when any of the three fails, and stay silent on a clean run.

options.text: Depend on all three tasks and run when all succeeded, after the report is built.
options.rationale: That runs the notification only when nothing failed, which reverses what the Failure constraints meant.

options.text: Make it the first task so that the owner is warned before anything can fail.
options.rationale: A first task would run on every night before any failure exists, so it carries no information.

options.text: Drop it, because the platform can retry failed tasks automatically.
options.rationale: A retry is not a message to the owner; the package promised a notification on failure.

questions.prompt: The watermark selects rows by updated_at, which an AFTER UPDATE trigger maintains. A correction to inspection 101 arrives through a load that runs with the trigger disabled. What happens tonight?

options.text: The watermark selects the row anyway because its values changed.
options.rationale: The selection compares timestamps, not values; nothing in the window query looks at units_defective.

options.text: The row receives a new identity value and appears as an extra inspection.
options.rationale: Identity values are assigned on insert; an update keeps the row's existing inspection_id.

options.text: The row keeps its old updated_at, the window never selects it, and its business day is not rebuilt.
options.rationale: The window reads only updated_at; a write path that skips the trigger changes values without leaving the signal the watermark uses.

options.text: The load fails, because the trigger is required for every write.
options.rationale: Writes succeed while a trigger is disabled; the silence is exactly the risk the inventory must record.

questions.prompt: The target writes detail, then report, then the watermark as three separate commits, and the job fails after the detail commit. Which design makes the retry safe?

options.text: Move the watermark first, so that the retry does not reprocess any rows.
options.rationale: The retry would then skip the failed window and leave the report stale with nothing left to trigger a rebuild.

options.text: Append the new report rows instead of replacing them, so that nothing is lost.
options.rationale: Appends are not idempotent: every retry would add another copy of the same groups.

options.text: Do nothing special, because every write on the target joins one transaction automatically.
options.rationale: Each table commit is atomic on its own; multi-statement transactions are a separate feature with requirements, in Public Preview when read.

options.text: Rebuild whole affected days from the same (since, until] window and move the watermark only after both tables are written.
options.rationale: Replacing whole days is idempotent, and an unmoved watermark makes the retry select the same work; Lab L24's retry converges to the legacy report.

questions.prompt: Tonight's window was recorded as (06:30 on 3 March, 06:30 on 4 March] when the run started. Inspection 112 was committed at 06:40 on 4 March while the run was still going, and the run finished at 06:45. What happens to 112?

options.text: Tonight's run selects it, because it was committed before the run finished.
options.rationale: Reading past the recorded until pulls in rows the legacy report never contained; Lab L24 flags exactly this on 4 March as a basis error.

options.text: The next window, which starts at 06:30 on 4 March, selects it, because tonight's window ends at the until recorded at the start.
options.rationale: The half-open window is fixed when the run starts; later rows wait for the next run, which begins exactly where this one ended, so nothing is skipped or read twice.

options.text: No run ever selects it, because the next window starts when this run finished.
options.rationale: The next window starts at the stored watermark, 06:30, not at the finish time, so 06:40 falls inside it.

options.text: Both runs select it, and the second rebuild overwrites the first.
options.rationale: Tonight's window excludes updated_at values after 06:30, so only the next window selects the row.

questions.prompt: A raw file value of 05:59:59.999 on 4 March is stored by the legacy DATETIME column and landed by the new path as TIMESTAMP_NTZ. With a 06:00 cutoff, which business days result?

options.text: Both 3 March, because both types keep milliseconds.
options.rationale: DATETIME cannot hold .999; its fractional seconds end in .000, .003 or .007.

options.text: Both 4 March, because TIMESTAMP_NTZ also rounds to .000, .003 or .007.
options.rationale: That rounding belongs to DATETIME; TIMESTAMP_NTZ stores the value as given.

options.text: Legacy 4 March and new path 3 March: DATETIME rounds .999 up to 06:00:00.000, TIMESTAMP_NTZ keeps it.
options.rationale: DATETIME stores 1/300-second increments and rounds the last half tick up; TIMESTAMP_NTZ keeps microseconds and has no zone.

options.text: Legacy 3 March and new path 4 March, because TIMESTAMP_NTZ applies the session time zone.
options.rationale: TIMESTAMP_NTZ carries no time zone and is computed without one.

questions.prompt: A translator moves s.plant_code = 'P1' from the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN into a WHERE filter after the join. Inspection 106 has a NULL inspector code. What happens to it?

options.text: It disappears: its joined columns are NULL, the WHERE predicate is not true, and the LEFT JOIN acts like an inner join.
options.rationale: WHERE runs after the join; NULL = 'P1' is unknown, so the row is filtered out before any COALESCE can label it UNASSIGNED.

options.text: It stays as UNASSIGNED, because a LEFT JOIN always keeps every left row.
options.rationale: A LEFT JOIN keeps left rows through the join; a later WHERE can still remove them.

options.text: It stays with a NULL shift, because COALESCE runs after WHERE.
options.rationale: The row is gone before the projection with COALESCE is evaluated, so there is nothing to label.

options.text: The query fails, because comparing with NULL raises an error in ANSI mode.
options.rationale: ANSI mode raises errors for invalid operations such as bad casts; a comparison with NULL returns NULL.

questions.prompt: Under the source's case-insensitive collation, which stored code does NOT equal 'QA07' in the join?

options.rationale: The CI collation treats upper and lower case as identical, so 'qa07' joins to QA07.

options.text: ' QA07', with a leading space.
options.rationale: Padding adds trailing spaces to the shorter string; a leading space is a real character, so the source keeps it distinct.

options.text: 'QA07 ', with a trailing space.
options.rationale: SQL Server pads the shorter string before comparing, so trailing spaces never count.
Mixed case is still case, and the CI collation ignores it.

questions.prompt: The new path stores each inspection as a correct UTC instant and computes to_date(ts - INTERVAL 6 HOURS) in a session whose time zone is UTC. For a New York plant in early March (UTC−5), where does the effective cutoff fall?

options.text: At 06:00 local time, because the stored instant is correct.
options.rationale: A correct instant still renders in the session zone when a date is taken from it.

options.text: At 11:00 local time.
options.rationale: The shift runs the other way: 06:00 UTC is five hours earlier in New York, not later.

options.text: Nowhere: TIMESTAMP values ignore time zones.
options.rationale: TIMESTAMP is shown in the session zone; TIMESTAMP_NTZ is the type computed without one.

options.text: At 01:00 local time: 06:00 UTC is 01:00 in New York, so rows between 01:00 and 06:00 move to the next day.
options.rationale: The date is taken in the session zone; Lab L24's session flip moves inspections 103 and 109 exactly this way.

selfQuestions.prompt: Decompose sp_daily_inspections into target steps. For each step, name its input, its output and the one test that would show it matches the legacy behaviour.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Step 1 selects rows with updated_at in (since, until] and returns affected business days; test: tonight returns 2, 3 and 4 March. Step 2 rebuilds whole affected days of detail with the collation key rule and the plant predicate in ON; test: detail keyed by inspection_id equals the legacy detail. Step 3 aggregates with div and DECIMAL; test: the report reconciles on keys, totals and types. Step 4 moves the watermark after both writes; test: a failure after the detail write leaves it unchanged and the retry converges.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each step owns one behaviour and one observable result, so a failed test points to one step. Splitting selection and rebuild differently is fine if every step keeps an executable check.

selfQuestions.prompt: sp_sensor_rollup fills a global temporary table that sp_line_summary reads from another session. How do you migrate that handoff, and what must the inventory record first?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Record the writer, the reader, the columns and when each runs, because a ##global table is visible to every session and exists only while referenced. On the target, tasks run in separate sessions, so a temporary view or session-scoped temporary table cannot carry it. Replace it with a named, owned table (or one task that runs both steps), add a dependency so the reader runs after the writer, and test that the reader sees exactly the writer's rows for one run.
selfQuestions.reasoning: A session-scoped object cannot cross tasks, so the hidden coupling becomes an explicit table and dependency. Merging both procedures into one task is acceptable when they always run together.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the basis statement and the checks, in order, that you would run before accepting one night of the P1 pilot.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Basis: P1 inspections only; rows updated at or before 06:30 on 4 March on both sides; business day at 06:00 on the New York server clock; NULL equals NULL and an empty string is not NULL. Checks in order: row counts for detail and report; keys by inspection_id and by plant, day and shift, listing only-old, only-new and changed fields; per-day totals of units, defective units and rework cost compared exactly; null counts per column; declared types. Accept only with no unexplained difference and every exception owned.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The basis removes differences that are not migration defects, and keys before totals stops a matching total from hiding moved rows. Adding a tolerance only for genuinely non-integer measures is an acceptable variation.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write a coexistence and cutover plan for the P1 report: what runs when, what opens the gate, and how you would roll back.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Coexistence: the legacy Agent job keeps feeding the morning report; the new job runs after it on the same as-of moment, writes to its own tables and reconciles every night. Gate: five consecutive clean days after the last code change, every explained difference owned, rollback rehearsed. Cutover: move consumers one report at a time and keep the legacy job scheduled through a rollback window, comparing outputs daily. Rollback: point consumers back to the legacy tables and pause the new job. Decommission only after the window closes, archiving the old outputs.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The old path stays the fallback until evidence accumulates, and the switch depends on stated criteria rather than a date. A longer parallel run is acceptable if capacity and cost allow.

beats.title: The old pipeline is a chain of promises, not a list of objects
beats.outcome: Trace Cinderline's nightly pipeline from correction file to report and record what an object list misses.
beats.explanation: Cinderline's morning quality report comes from a SQL Server Agent job at 06:30 that runs an SSIS-style package: a loop loads correction files, one Execute SQL Task applies them and another calls the stored procedure sp_daily_inspections. A [[dbxfe-sqlserver-inventory-concept|migration inventory]] records that chain and what each step promises. Notice in the second state what an object list misses: the server clock that places the 06:00 cutoff, the collation that decides which codes join, and the watermark that decides which rows a run reads.

handbook.markdown:
An inventory is the list you check the migration against, so it must hold what decides results, not only what exists. For sp_daily_inspections, Lab L24's text scanner and a reading by hand agree: four tables read (erp.inspection, erp.inspector, etl.watermark, dbo.rpt_quality_detail), three written, one temporary table (#affected_days), GETDATE() as the only clock, one `DATEADD(HOUR, -6, ...)` cutoff, one INT / INT rate, seven string-key comparisons decided by the collation, one ISNULL replacement, two predicates inside a LEFT JOIN's ON clause, etl.watermark as state, and one transaction around DELETE, INSERT, MERGE and UPDATE.

Then add what text cannot show, asking the owners:

```text
Workload    sp_daily_inspections (P1 morning report)
Schedule    Agent job nightly_quality, 06:30 on the server clock (America/New_York)
Settings    CI_AS collation on key columns; ANSI_NULLS saved with the procedure
State       etl.watermark, moved inside the transaction
Writers     ERP screen (fires the trigger), correction load (does it?)
Readers     morning report, quality workbook (owner unconfirmed)
Unknowns    may change tracking be enabled? who owns the workbook?
```

A regular-expression scan misses dynamic SQL, synonyms, views and callers, so treat it as a first draft the owner confirms. The inventory also picks the pilot: bounded to one plant, representative of the hard features (collation keys, a cutoff, incremental state), reconcilable against an existing report, and a read path you can reverse. The Migration inventory field guide holds the template.

beats.recap: Inventory the settings that decide results (clock, collation, watermark), not only the objects that exist.
beats.hint: Ask what would change the numbers if it were different, not what exists.

beats.title: Code that compiles can still mean something else
beats.outcome: Predict which reconciliation check catches each difference between a line-by-line translation and the legacy procedure.
beats.explanation: A line-by-line translation of sp_daily_inspections compiles on Spark and returns six report rows, exactly like the legacy job. [[dbxfe-sqlserver-equivalence-concept|Semantic equivalence]] asks a different question: the same rows and values on the same basis. Notice in the first two states how 3 March differs: DAY shrinks, UNASSIGNED disappears, rates gain decimals and money gains binary noise. The third state shows why evidence needs several checks: the report row count passes while keys, totals, nulls and types all fail.

handbook.markdown:
Syntax conversion rewrites text; semantic migration preserves behaviour. Lab L24 makes the difference executable. Its target and its naive translation share every line except five decisions:

```python
TARGET = Rules(key_rule="collation", join_rule="on", day_rule="server_local",
               division="integer", amount_type="decimal")
NAIVE  = Rules(key_rule="binary",    join_rule="where", day_rule="session",
               division="fractional", amount_type="double")
```

Each naive choice is what a careful line-by-line reader would write: `==` for `=`, a filter gathered into one `where`, `to_date(ts - INTERVAL 6 HOURS)` for the DATEADD, `/` for `/`, and a DOUBLE for a number. Run on local Spark 4.0.4 against the same synthetic extract, the naive path keeps 7 of 11 detail rows, moves two to a later day, and still returns six report rows. Flipping one choice at a time assigns each defect to the check that owns it: binary keys fail only the keyed comparisons; the WHERE filter also fails the null count; the session day fails keys and totals; fractional division fails report values and types; DOUBLE money fails types and exact totals.

When is a translation good enough? Only when every check passes on a stated basis, or every difference is registered and owned. A converter's 'zero errors' and equal row counts establish neither. To demonstrate this honestly, say what ran: local Spark with synthetic fixtures, and legacy results derived from the procedure text and the documented type behaviour, not from a SQL Server.

beats.recap: Equal row counts and a clean compile prove nothing; five semantic choices decide whether the report means the same thing.

beats.title: A stored procedure is several steps sharing one name
beats.outcome: Split a stored procedure into target steps that each have one input, one output and one executable check.
beats.explanation: sp_daily_inspections reads the watermark, collects affected days in a temporary table, rebuilds detail, merges the report and moves the watermark, all inside one transaction. [[dbxfe-sqlserver-decomposition-concept|Decomposition]] turns that block into steps you can test one at a time. Notice in the second state that the watermark step is marked as a warning: on the target it must run last, after both writes. The reconcile step is new, because the legacy job never checked its own output.

handbook.markdown:
Decompose along the procedure's real seams: selection, rules, writes and state. For the pilot that gives four functions, each with a test Lab L24 runs:

```python
days = affected_days(spark, rows, "P1", since, until)      # [["P1","2026-03-02"], ...]
detail, report = build(spark, rows, "P1", TARGET, as_of=until, days=[d for _, d in days])
state["detail"] = keep_other_days(state["detail"]) + rows_of(detail)
state["report"] = keep_other_days(state["report"]) + rows_of(report)
state["watermark"] = until                                  # last, after both writes
```

Replacing whole affected days is what the procedure's DELETE and INSERT did, and it makes retries idempotent. The procedure's MERGE never deletes a group that disappears after a correction; the target's day replacement does. No fixture exercises that difference, so it is written into the inventory as a known behaviour change to confirm with the report owner.

On Databricks the rebuild can use MERGE INTO on a Delta table, which fails with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE when two source rows match one target row, or a replace of the affected partitions. Keep business rules (key normalization, the cutoff, the rate) in named functions so the same rule serves every step.

When not to decompose: a procedure that only wraps one SELECT for a report can become a view or a single query. Decompose when the procedure mixes state, rules and writes, which is when a single translated block cannot tell you where a difference came from.

beats.recap: One test per step turns 'the report is wrong' into 'the window step missed 2 March'.

samajh.text: Socho dadi ne ek hi parchi par poore din ka kaam likh diya: doodh lao, bijli ka bill bharo, aur agar bill counter band ho to pehle sabzi le aao. Ek parchi hai, par andar teen alag kaam aur ek chhupi hui shart hai. Agar shaam ko doodh nahi aaya, to poori parchi ko dosh doge ya us ek kaam ko dhoondhoge? Kaam alag-alag likho, har kaam ka nateeja check karo.
samajh.mapping: The single note is the stored procedure, each errand is a target step with its own input and output, and the hidden condition is control flow that must become an explicit rule.
samajh.boundary: Errands can run in any order, but the watermark step must run after both writes; the analogy says nothing about ordering or retries.

beats.title: Precedence constraints become dependencies with conditions
beats.outcome: Map an SSIS-style control flow and its Agent schedule onto job tasks, dependencies, run-if conditions and a schedule with a time zone.
beats.explanation: The package runs a file loop, applies corrections, builds the report and mails the owner if anything fails. In [[dbxfe-sqlserver-orchestration-concept|control-flow mapping]], Success constraints become dependencies that run when all succeeded, and the three Failure constraints joined by OR become one task that runs when at least one dependency failed. Notice in the second state that the schedule gains the time zone the Agent job never wrote down; the job plan names it instead of inheriting a default.

handbook.markdown:
Map each promise of the control flow, not each box:

| SSIS-style element | Job plan element |
|---|---|
| Foreach Loop + Data Flow Task | one ingestion task; a file-arrival trigger or incremental file ingestion if files arrive irregularly |
| Execute SQL Task | a task running the decomposed steps |
| Success constraint | dependency, run if all succeeded |
| Failure constraints joined by OR | one task depending on all of them, run if at least one failed |
| Agent schedule 06:30 | schedule trigger at 06:30 America/New_York |
| Package parameters, catalog environments | job parameters and configuration |

Lab L24's `map_package()` produces that plan from the package outline:

```json
{"task_key": "notify_on_failure", "source": "Send Mail Task",
 "depends_on": ["apply_corrections", "build_daily_report", "loop_over_delivered_csv_files"],
 "run_if": "at_least_one_failed"}
```

Check two things in the current Lakeflow Jobs documentation before relying on the plan: how skipped and upstream-failed tasks count for each run-if condition, and how the schedule records its time zone. The plan was not deployed. Agent schedules run on the server clock, which moves with daylight saving; name the zone so the target keeps the same local time.

What fails: mapping the mail task to 'all succeeded' (it would mail only on success), dropping it because retries exist (a retry is not a message), and chaining two Agent jobs by start time instead of by dependency, which works until one runs long.

beats.recap: Success edges become dependencies; OR-joined failure edges become one 'at least one failed' task; schedules name their zone.

beats.title: Identity columns and triggers are behaviour the table hides
beats.outcome: Recognize how identity values and a trigger-maintained timestamp shape keys and incremental selection, and what breaks when a write path skips the trigger.
beats.explanation: inspection_id is an [[dbxfe-sqlserver-identity-concept|identity column]]: unique, assigned on insert, and allowed to have gaps, on SQL Server and on a Delta identity column alike. updated_at is kept by a [[dbxfe-sqlserver-trigger-concept|DML trigger]], and the watermark trusts it. Notice in the second state that a correction loaded with the trigger disabled changes the values but not updated_at, so tonight's window never sees it and 2 March is never rebuilt.

handbook.markdown:
Identity values are keys, not counters. SQL Server documents that consecutive values are not guaranteed and that cached values can be lost after a restart, so gaps are normal. Carry the source key across unchanged during migration; never regenerate it on the target, or every reconciliation keyed by inspection_id breaks. If the target table needs its own surrogate for new rows, Delta identity columns are BIGINT only, unique but not necessarily consecutive, and declaring one disables concurrent transactions on the table. `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` lets a load supply the existing values; `GENERATED ALWAYS` refuses them.

Triggers are code that runs on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. For every trigger on a source table, the inventory records what it writes and which write paths fire it:

```sql
-- the kind of trigger the watermark depends on (teaching text, not executed)
CREATE TRIGGER erp.trg_inspection_touch ON erp.inspection AFTER UPDATE AS
  UPDATE i SET updated_at = GETDATE()
    FROM erp.inspection AS i JOIN inserted AS n ON n.inspection_id = i.inspection_id;
```

On the target there is no trigger to inherit: either the ingestion computes the change signal itself, or a change feed such as change tracking supplies it. Inspect for three failures: a write path that runs with triggers disabled, a trigger that writes to another table the inventory missed, and an INSTEAD OF trigger that silently rewrites what a writer sent. Each shows up in reconciliation as values that differ while every timestamp looks right.

beats.recap: Carry identity keys unchanged and treat every trigger as code the target must replace or make unnecessary.
beats.hint: Ask which column the watermark reads, then ask what writes that column.

beats.title: One transaction becomes three commits and a retry rule
beats.outcome: Replace a multi-table transaction with idempotent day rebuilds and a watermark moved last, or name the conditions for a multi-statement transaction.
beats.explanation: The legacy job changes detail, report and watermark inside one [[dbxfe-sqlserver-transaction-concept|transaction]], so readers never see half a run. On the target each table commits on its own. Notice in the second state that a failure after the detail write leaves new detail beside an old report while the watermark stays put; in the third, the retry selects the same window, rebuilds the same days and only then moves the watermark, so the result converges to the legacy report.

handbook.markdown:
`BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT` with `SET XACT_ABORT ON` gave the legacy job all-or-nothing writes: any runtime error rolled back the detail rebuild, the MERGE and the watermark together. Readers under READ COMMITTED never saw the half-built report; whether they waited on locks or read row versions depended on the READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT setting, which the inventory records.

On a Delta target each table write is its own atomic commit and readers see the last committed version. Two designs replace the old guarantee:

1. **Idempotent rebuild, watermark last.** Recompute whole affected days from the same (since, until] window, write detail, write report, then advance the watermark. A failure anywhere leaves the watermark unmoved, so the retry repeats the same work and converges. Lab L24 injects a failure after the detail write: the watermark stays at 2026-03-03 06:30, the report is inconsistent with the detail for a moment, and the retry reconciles with the legacy report.
2. **Multi-statement transaction.** Databricks documents BEGIN ATOMIC ... END and interactive BEGIN TRANSACTION, all tables Unity Catalog managed tables; it was in Public Preview for managed Delta tables when read, so it is a verification item, not an assumption.

What fails: appending report rows (a retry duplicates them), moving the watermark first (a failed run is skipped forever), and treating a consistent-looking table as proof (check that the report equals the aggregate of the detail). Concurrent writers matter too: Delta's default WriteSerializable isolation lets blind appends proceed but can reject concurrent MERGE operations on the same data, so schedule the rebuild so it does not overlap another writer.

beats.recap: Without one transaction, make every step repeatable and move the watermark only after the writes it describes.

beats.title: Temporary objects cannot cross a task boundary
beats.outcome: Classify each temporary object as task-local or a hidden handoff, and give each handoff a named, owned home on the target.
beats.explanation: #affected_days is a local [[dbxfe-sqlserver-temp-concept|temporary object]]: visible to one session and dropped when the procedure ends, so on the target it becomes a DataFrame or temporary view inside one task. Notice in the first state the ##global table that another procedure reads from a different session. Tasks on the target do not share sessions, so that handoff becomes a named table with an owner and an explicit dependency between the two tasks.

handbook.markdown:
SQL Server offers local temporary tables (`#name`, one session, dropped with the session or the procedure that created them) and global ones (`##name`, visible to every session). Search the inventory for both prefixes and classify each object:

| Object | Scope in the source | Target home |
|---|---|---|
| `#affected_days` | one procedure run | a DataFrame or temporary view inside the task |
| `##line_handoff` | shared between two procedures | a named, owned table plus a task dependency |
| a temporary table added for an index | one run, for speed | usually nothing: test whether the query needs it |

On Databricks, temporary views and temporary tables are session-scoped: a temporary table lives only in the session that created it and is dropped when that session ends (at most seven days). Two tasks in a job do not share that session, so neither can carry a handoff.

```python
affected = silver.where(changed_in_window).select("plant_code", "business_day").distinct()
affected.createOrReplaceTempView("affected_days")   # visible inside this task only
```

A global temporary table is the migration's hidden coupling: sp_line_summary quietly depends on sp_sensor_rollup having run first in the same window. Making it a named table forces the questions the source never answered: who owns it, what its columns mean, how long it is kept, and what happens when the writer fails. What to inspect: tempdb-heavy procedures, objects created in one procedure and read in another, and reports that read a temporary table indirectly through a view.

beats.recap: A local temporary table stays inside its task; a global one becomes a named table with an owner and a dependency.

beats.title: A watermark selects by change time, and it cannot see a delete
beats.outcome: Define an incremental window that selects late corrections, keeps the as-of basis and names what a timestamp watermark cannot see.
beats.explanation: etl.watermark is the job's [[dbxfe-sqlserver-watermark-concept|watermark]]: tonight reads rows whose updated_at falls after 06:30 on 3 March and up to 06:30 on 4 March. Notice in the first state that inspection 101, inspected on 2 March, is selected because it was corrected at 16:00; in the second, selecting by inspected_at loses it. The third state shows a delete, which leaves no timestamp at all; [[dbxfe-sqlserver-tracking-concept|change tracking]] records the deleted key.

handbook.markdown:
The window is half-open, `updated_at > since AND updated_at <= until`, with `until` recorded once at the start of the run. A row updated exactly at `since` belongs to the previous run; a row committed after `until` (inspection 112 at 06:40) waits for the next. Rebuilding every business day the selected rows touch, rather than appending the rows, is what makes a late correction safe:

```python
changed = silver.where((F.col("updated_local") > since) & (F.col("updated_local") <= until))
days = changed.select("plant_code", "business_day").distinct()   # 2, 3 and 4 March tonight
```

Three things a timestamp watermark cannot do. It cannot see a delete, because the row and its timestamp are gone. It cannot see a change made by a path that skips the trigger. And it can miss a change whose transaction started before `until` but committed after the run read the table, because that row's updated_at falls inside a window already processed. SQL Server's change tracking records which rows changed, including deletes, ordered by transaction commit, which the documentation describes as reliable with long-running and overlapping transactions; change data capture reads the changed values from the transaction log. The Lakeflow Connect SQL Server connector ingests incrementally with either and recommends change tracking for tables with a primary key; its availability, networking and source versions are verification items for the design review, not assumptions.

When not to use a watermark: a small table that can be reloaded in full every night is simpler and cannot miss anything. What to inspect: rows updated in the minutes around `until`, days rebuilt per run, and a periodic full comparison that would reveal a missed delete.

beats.recap: Select by change time in a half-open window, rebuild whole days, and name deletes as the watermark's blind spot.

beats.title: Every source data type carries a rule the target must choose
beats.outcome: Map DATETIME, DECIMAL, integer division and NVARCHAR to target types and name the check that proves each choice.
beats.explanation: Data types decide results, not just storage. [[dbxfe-sqlserver-datetime-concept|DATETIME]] is local, has no offset and rounds to 1/300 second; INT / INT truncates; [[dbxfe-sqlserver-decimal-concept|DECIMAL money]] stays exact. Notice in the second state that one raw value, 05:59:59.999, lands on 3 March as TIMESTAMP_NTZ but on 4 March once DATETIME rounds it, and that 400 / 120 is 3 in T-SQL but 3.3333333333333335 with Spark's slash. The third state writes the integer rate out.

handbook.markdown:
Choose each target type for the behaviour you must keep, then test that behaviour:

| Source | Behaviour | Target choice | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| DATETIME | local wall clock, no offset, 1/300 s | TIMESTAMP_NTZ plus an explicit clock rule | business day per row |
| DECIMAL(12,2) | exact | DECIMAL(12,2); SUM widens to DECIMAL(22,2) in Spark | exact totals |
| INT / INT | truncates | `div`, which returns BIGINT | rate per group |
| NVARCHAR(20) under CI_AS | collation equality, declared length | STRING plus a key rule | key profile, length check |

Worked numbers from Lab L24: 800 / 300 is 2 in T-SQL, 2.6666666666666665 with Spark's `/` and 2 with `div`. Money as DOUBLE prints 0.30000000000000004 for 0.10 + 0.20 and 2.9000000000000004 for 2.20 + 0.70, while 8.35 happens to print exactly, so a DOUBLE column can pass most rows and fail a few. The type check catches the column before anyone argues about a tolerance.

The rounding matters at boundaries. A raw file value of 05:59:59.999 is 05:59:59.999 as TIMESTAMP_NTZ (business day 3 March) but 06:00:00.000 once stored as DATETIME (business day 4 March). If the new path reads the upstream file while the old path reads the DATETIME column, the two paths disagree on exactly those rows; land from the same source during reconciliation, or register the difference.

Under Spark 4's default ANSI mode an invalid cast or an integer overflow raises an error rather than returning NULL, so a type mismatch surfaces as a failed run, not as quietly missing values. NVARCHAR holds Unicode text: check that the export and the landing keep every character (a lossy code-page conversion silently replaces what it cannot represent), and that any length rule a consumer relies on counts characters, not bytes.

beats.recap: Pick the target type for the behaviour to keep: NTZ plus a clock, exact decimals, div for integer rates.

beats.title: A filter's position decides whether NULL rows survive
beats.outcome: Predict how an outer join, a function or NOT IN behaves with NULL on each engine and choose the equivalent form.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-sqlserver-nulls-concept|NULL semantics]] mostly agree between SQL Server and Spark and differ in the corners translations hit. Notice in the first two states that keeping the plant predicate in the ON clause leaves inspections 106 and 111 as UNASSIGNED, while moving it to WHERE removes them, because the predicate is not true for NULL joined columns. The third state shows two same-named functions: T-SQL CONCAT treats NULL as empty, Spark's concat returns NULL.

handbook.markdown:
Four corners to check in every translated procedure:

1. **Outer-join filters.** A predicate on the joined table belongs in ON. In WHERE it removes the rows the LEFT JOIN was written to keep. Lab L24's WHERE flip drops inspections 106 and 111, removes 3 March UNASSIGNED from the report and changes the null count of inspector_code from 1 to 0.
2. **Same-named functions.** `CONCAT('P1', '-', NULL)` is 'P1-' in T-SQL and NULL with Spark's `concat`; `concat_ws` or explicit `coalesce` reproduces the T-SQL result. If such a string becomes a join key, the NULL silently removes matches.
3. **NOT IN.** Both engines return no rows for `x NOT IN (1, NULL)`. A 'faster' rewrite as a left anti join keeps `x = 2`, so the rewrite, not the engine, changes the answer.
4. **Saved settings.** SQL Server stores the ANSI_NULLS and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER settings with each procedure when it is created. A legacy procedure created with ANSI_NULLS OFF treats `column = @var` as true when both are NULL; find those in the inventory before assuming standard behaviour.

```python
spark.sql("SELECT concat('P1','-',CAST(NULL AS STRING)) AS c, "
          "concat_ws('', 'P1','-',CAST(NULL AS STRING)) AS w").first()   # c=None, w='P1-'
```

For key comparisons where NULL must match NULL, use Spark's null-safe `<=>` (`eqNullSafe`) and state the null rule in the reconciliation basis. Spark's comparison with NULL returns NULL rather than an error, even in ANSI mode.

beats.recap: Keep outer-join filters in ON, check same-named functions for NULL rules, and never rewrite NOT IN as an anti join blindly.

beats.title: The collation, not the data, decides which keys are equal
beats.outcome: Reproduce a case-insensitive, trailing-space-insensitive join and prove the rule with a key profile.
beats.explanation: Under the source [[dbxfe-sqlserver-collation-concept|collation]], 'qa07' and 'QA07 ' equal 'QA07': SQL Server pads trailing spaces before comparing and CI ignores case. Spark compares bytes. Notice in the first state that upper(rtrim()) matches the source on every row while trim wrongly equates ' QA07', whose leading space the source keeps. The second state is the profile that tells you which columns need a rule and which data would catch the wrong one.

handbook.markdown:
Equality in the source is a property of the collation, so the target must choose a rule and prove it. For ASCII codes under a case-insensitive collation, `upper(rtrim(code))` on both sides reproduces the join:

```python
same_code = F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("i.inspector_code"))) == F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("s.inspector_code")))
```

Profile before choosing. Lab L24 counts, per column, the rows whose raw value differs from the rule's form and the rows with a leading space: inspector_code in P1 has 2 case or trailing-space variants, plant_code none, and P2 has one leading-space code. The P1 data cannot tell `rtrim` from `trim`; only P2's ' QA21' can, which is why a transfer fixture exists.

The collation also changes grouping and uniqueness. GROUP BY on a case-insensitive column puts 'qa07' and 'QA07' in one group, and a unique constraint rejects the second spelling; on the target, group by the normalized key and test uniqueness on it. Accent and width sensitivity, non-ASCII case rules and sort order are separate settings; this emulation covers none of them.

Databricks can also attach a collation to a string column: UTF8_LCASE compares case-insensitively after lower-casing and keeps accents distinct, and Databricks recommends it for migrations from systems with simple case-insensitive matching. Whether it treats trailing spaces as the source does is a separate question to verify for your runtime before replacing the explicit rule.

beats.recap: Reproduce the collation with an explicit key rule, prove it with a profile, and group by the normalized key.

samajh.text: Class mein teacher attendance leti hai. Register mein kisi ne 'ravi' likha, kisi ne 'Ravi ', aur teacher teeno ko ek hi bachcha maanti hai kyunki unka niyam hai: bade-chhote akshar aur peeche ki khali jagah ginti mein nahi. Par agar naam ke aage jagah ho, ' Ravi', to woh use alag maanti hai. Naya school software har naam ko akshar-dar-akshar milata hai, to teacher ka niyam likh ke dena padega.

samajh.boundary: A teacher can use judgement for odd names; a database applies the collation mechanically, including to codes nobody has seen yet.

beats.title: A business day belongs to a named clock
beats.outcome: Compute a business day that no session setting can move, and recognize when the intended clock differs from the legacy one.
beats.explanation: The legacy [[dbxfe-sqlserver-businessday-concept|business day]] is wall-clock time on the New York server minus six hours. Notice in the first state that 02:10 on 3 March belongs to 2 March and 06:00:00.000 on 4 March to 4 March. In the second, the same instants dated in a UTC session move the cutoff to 01:00 local. The third shows plant P2 in Chicago, where the intended 06:00 plant-local rule moves two rows a day earlier: a registered change, not a defect.

handbook.markdown:
`CAST(DATEADD(HOUR, -6, inspected_at) AS DATE)` has no zone in it, because DATETIME has none; the zone is the server's clock, and GETDATE() returns it. The target must write that clock down:

```python
local = F.col("inspected_at").cast("timestamp_ntz")                 # server wall clock
server_day = F.to_date(local - F.expr("INTERVAL 6 HOURS"))          # legacy rule
plant_day = F.to_date(F.convert_timezone(F.lit("America/New_York"),
                     F.lit("America/Chicago"), local) - F.expr("INTERVAL 6 HOURS"))
```

TIMESTAMP_NTZ arithmetic ignores the session, so `server_day` is the same under UTC, Asia/Kolkata or any other session zone; Lab L24 checks this. A TIMESTAMP holds an instant and is dated in the session zone, whose Databricks default is UTC; in early March New York is UTC−5, so dating instants in UTC moves the 06:00 cutoff to 01:00 local and inspections 103 and 109 land a day late. The same code is right under an America/New_York session, which is exactly why a session setting must not carry a business rule.

The intended rule may differ from the legacy one. P2's rows carry New York time, so the legacy cutoff is 05:00 in Chicago; under the plant-local rule, inspections at 06:05 and 06:25 New York time move from 11 to 10 March. That is a business change: register it with an owner, run it as an expected difference, and do not ship it silently inside the migration. Daylight saving moves both zones on the same US weekend here; for plants in other countries, test the transition dates explicitly.

beats.recap: Store the wall clock as TIMESTAMP_NTZ, name the zone in the rule, and treat a new cutoff as an owned change.

beats.title: Align the basis, compare keys, then totals
beats.outcome: Write a basis statement and run counts, keys, totals, nulls and types in an order that cannot hide moved rows.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-sqlserver-reconciliation-concept|Reconciliation]] compares two paths on one basis: the same population, as-of moment, day rule and null rule. Notice in the second state that with binary keys the row counts and the 3 March total agree while DAY and UNASSIGNED do not; a totals-first check would have passed. The third state shows the other outcome: differences that an owned register entry predicts, re-derived with no residue, which makes the verdict explained rather than ignored.

handbook.markdown:
Fix the basis before comparing anything. Lab L24's basis is P1 only, rows updated at or before 06:30 on 4 March, business day at 06:00 on the server clock, NULL equals NULL. Leaving out the as-of filter adds inspection 112 (updated at 06:40) to 4 March DAY: a basis error, not a migration defect.

Then run the checks in an order where each one explains the next:

1. Row counts for detail and report (necessary, never sufficient).
2. Keys: only-old, only-new and changed fields, keyed by inspection_id and by plant, day and shift.
3. Totals per plant and day, compared exactly for integers and DECIMAL money; every difference must trace to a keyed difference.
4. Null counts per column, old against new.
5. Declared types: integral where the source was INT, DECIMAL with the same scale for money.

```python
cond = old["plant_code"].eqNullSafe(new["plant_code"]) & old["business_day"].eqNullSafe(new["business_day"]) \
     & old["shift_code"].eqNullSafe(new["shift_code"])
joined = old.join(new, cond, "full_outer")   # only-old, only-new and both, the form that scales
```

A tolerance is a decision made before the run, only for genuinely non-integer measures; none is needed here. Differences a rule change causes go into a register with an owner; the plant-local rule's two moves are accepted only because re-deriving the legacy report with them applied equals the new report exactly. Remove the owner and the same differences fail. Tools such as Lakebridge's reconcile can automate comparisons; they do not choose the basis or own the exceptions. The Reconciliation plan field guide holds the template.

beats.recap: Basis first, keys before totals, exact thresholds stated in advance, and every accepted difference owned.

Pehle dekhte ho kaun si cheez sirf uski copy mein hai, kaun si sirf aapki diary mein, aur kis cheez ki keemat alag hai. Total baad mein. Kyunki ho sakta hai usne chawal do baar likhe aur daal likhna bhool gaya, aur total phir bhi barabar aa jaaye.

beats.title: Evidence, not the calendar, opens the cutover gate
beats.outcome: Plan coexistence, a cutover gate and a rollback path for one report, and explain why a code change restarts the count.
beats.explanation: During [[dbxfe-sqlserver-coexistence-concept|coexistence]] the legacy job keeps serving the morning report while the new job runs after it and reconciles nightly. Notice in the second state that the count of clean days starts again at the code change on 11 March and resets when an exception has no owner. [[dbxfe-sqlserver-cutover-concept|Cutover]] then moves consumers report by report, with the legacy schedule kept until the rollback window closes.

handbook.markdown:
Coexistence needs its own schedule design. The new job runs after the legacy job has finished, reads the same as-of moment, writes to its own tables and never feeds users. Both schedules name their time zone, and the reconciliation runs as the new job's last task, so a failed comparison is visible the same morning.

The gate is a rule written before the parallel run starts. Lab L24's version: five consecutive clean days since the last code change, where a day is clean if it passed or if every explained difference has a named owner, plus a rehearsed rollback. On the logged run, the pass on 9 March does not count (the code changed on 11 March); 11, 12 and 13 March qualify; 16 March carries an exception with no owner, so the count returns to zero and the gate stays closed. With the owner named and 17 March clean, the gate opens; without a rehearsed rollback it stays closed however many days pass.

Cutover moves consumers one report at a time. Keep the legacy job scheduled through a rollback window, compare outputs daily, and rehearse the switch back: point the report at the legacy tables and pause the new job. Decommission only when the window closes, and archive the last legacy outputs as reconciliation evidence.

When not to cut over: when an owner has not accepted a registered difference, when the source team cannot support the parallel run's extra reads, or when the only evidence is elapsed time. Say so in the decision record rather than letting a date decide. The Cutover and rollback plan field guide lists the entry conditions, decision owners, rollback triggers and rehearsal record in full.

beats.recap: Run both paths, count clean days only after the last change, own every exception, and keep the old path as the rollback.

extensionCards.prompt: Can a T-SQL stored procedure simply become a Databricks SQL stored procedure?
extensionCards.answer: Databricks can store SQL procedures in Unity Catalog and run them with CALL, but the body must still be rewritten in Databricks SQL and tested step by step.
extensionCards.explanation: CREATE PROCEDURE in Databricks defines a [[dbxfe-sqlserver-extension-procedures-concept|stored procedure]] in Unity Catalog with parameters and a body of SQL statements, on Databricks Runtime 17.0 or later; its release status and supported statements are verified for the workspace, not assumed. Keeping one procedure can suit teams that call it from tools, but it keeps every hidden rule in one block: collation, clocks and integer division still have to be reproduced explicitly, and a single block still cannot tell you which step caused a difference. A common compromise is a thin procedure that calls tested, named steps.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It separates a packaging choice (one procedure or several tasks) from the semantic work that neither choice avoids.

extensionCards.prompt: When can a multi-statement transaction replace the idempotent-retry design on Databricks?
extensionCards.answer: When every table written is a Unity Catalog managed table and the feature, in Public Preview for managed Delta tables when read, is available on the chosen compute.
extensionCards.explanation: Databricks documents non-interactive [[dbxfe-sqlserver-extension-transactions-concept|multi-statement transactions]] with BEGIN ATOMIC ... END, which commit automatically when every statement succeeds, and interactive BEGIN TRANSACTION on SQL warehouses; if a statement fails, all changes roll back. That restores the legacy all-or-nothing write of detail, report and watermark. Because it is a preview feature with table and compute requirements, the pilot keeps the idempotent design as the baseline and treats the transaction as an upgrade to verify; the rebuild-whole-days rule stays useful either way, because it makes reruns safe.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It shows when the legacy transaction guarantee can be restored directly and why the retry design remains the safe default.

extensionCards.prompt: Could a UTF8_LCASE collation replace the explicit upper(rtrim()) key rule?
extensionCards.answer: It gives case-insensitive comparison natively, but trailing-space behaviour, accents and runtime support must be checked and proven with the key profile first.
extensionCards.explanation: Databricks' [[dbxfe-sqlserver-extension-collation-concept|UTF8_LCASE collation]] compares strings after lower-casing them and keeps accented characters distinct, and Databricks recommends it for migrations from systems with simple case-insensitive matching. The source collation also ignores trailing spaces and keeps leading ones, so the replacement is only equivalent if the target collation treats spaces the same way; check the collation reference for your runtime, then rerun the key profile and the keyed reconciliation. Until both pass, the explicit rule is the proven one.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It names the native alternative to a hand-written key rule and the evidence required before switching.

extensionCards.prompt: What can a migration toolkit such as Lakebridge do, and what can it not establish?
extensionCards.answer: It can analyze source metadata and dependencies, transpile SQL and reconcile source and target data, but it cannot establish that a translation means the same thing on data nobody compared.
extensionCards.explanation: [[dbxfe-sqlserver-extension-lakebridge-concept|Lakebridge]] is a Databricks Labs toolkit with analyze, transpile and reconcile commands: the analyzer extracts metadata, lineage and dependencies, the transpiler converts legacy SQL to Databricks SQL, and the reconciler compares source and target data. That speeds up the inventory and the comparisons, but the basis, the thresholds, the semantic decisions and the owners of each exception remain the team's work. As a Labs project its support status and supported dialects are checked before relying on it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It places automated conversion and comparison inside the method instead of letting them stand in for it.

recap.title: Syntax converts; meaning has to be proven
recap.markdown: **Inventory what decides results, decompose the procedure into tested steps, and reconcile before you believe.** The Cinderline job's meaning lives in its collation, its outer-join filters, the clock behind the business day, integer division, exact money, its trigger and watermark, and the transaction around its writes. A line-by-line translation compiled, returned six report rows and failed every other check; five explicit choices made the target reconcile. Coexistence, owned exceptions and a rehearsed rollback turn that evidence into a cutover. **Transfer challenge:** a second report divides rework cost by defective units and groups by lot codes that arrive in mixed case; list the source rules you must inventory, the target choice for each, and the check that would catch a wrong one.

appliedTask.title: Migrate the P2 report without losing a row
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline adds plant P2 to the pilot. Its rows are stamped on the New York server although the plant is in Chicago; one inspector code arrives with a leading space and another in lower case with trailing spaces; the quality lead wants the business day to start at 06:00 plant time; and the ERP team now deletes test inspections every Friday. Change tracking has been approved for erp.inspection only. Describe the target choices for keys, the business day and incremental selection, the reconciliation you would run, and what must be true before P2 cuts over.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Keys: upper(rtrim()) on both sides, so 'qa22  ' joins QA22 and ' QA21' stays UNASSIGNED as it does in the source; the P2 key profile (one variant, one leading space) proves the rule, and a trim rule would fail the keyed comparison while day totals match. Business day: land the New York wall clock as TIMESTAMP_NTZ; reproduce the legacy server-clock cutoff first so the P2 reconciliation passes, then apply convert_timezone to America/Chicago as a registered change owned by the quality lead, which moves the 06:05 and 06:25 rows to 10 March and nothing else. Incremental: move erp.inspection to change tracking so Friday's deletes are seen; keep the half-open window and whole-day rebuilds. Reconciliation: counts, keys, totals, nulls and types on the stated basis, with the register explaining exactly the two moves. Cutover: five clean days after the last change, owned exceptions, rehearsed rollback.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer reproduces the legacy meaning before changing it, separates the owned rule change from migration defects, closes the delete blind spot with change tracking, and ties P2's cutover to the same evidence as P1.
